stem: A 36-year-old woman has had 8 months of exertional dyspnea and fatigue. She has a loud pulmonic component of S2 and a right ventricular heave. Right heart catheterization shows a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 42 mm Hg with a normal wedge pressure, and no cause for secondary disease is found. An oral drug is started, and she is told that she will need monthly liver tests and pregnancy tests.
oneliner: 36F + 8 mo exertional dyspnea + loud P2, RV heave + mean PA pressure 42, normal wedge + oral drug with monthly LFTs and pregnancy tests → antagonizes which mediator?
ask: The drug most likely blocks the action of which of the following mediators?

whyNot.A: **Prostacyclin**: a pulmonary **vasodilator**; blocking it would worsen disease (analogs such as treprostinil are used)
whyNot.B: **Nitric oxide**: a vasodilator; PDE-5 inhibitors boost its effect, not block it
whyNot.C: **Angiotensin II**: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are not the oral drugs used for this disease
whyNot.E: **Thromboxane A2**: its blockade (aspirin) would not need liver and pregnancy monitoring

why: **Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension treated with an oral drug that requires LFT and pregnancy monitoring** = **bosentan**, which blocks **endothelin-1** receptors (a potent vasoconstrictor and mitogen).

drug.name: Bosentan
drug.how: Blocks ETA/ETB receptors, reducing endothelin-1 vasoconstriction and proliferation
drug.watch: Hepatotoxicity (monthly LFTs), teratogenic (pregnancy tests), edema, anemia

stem: A 23-year-old woman with persistent asthma still wheezes several nights a week despite a daily inhaled corticosteroid. Her physician adds a once-daily tablet that is not a bronchodilator. On treatment, her urinary leukotriene E4 level is unchanged, but her night-time symptoms fall.
oneliner: 23F + persistent asthma on inhaled steroid + added once-daily non-bronchodilator tablet + urinary LTE4 unchanged + fewer night symptoms → molecular target?
ask: The added tablet acts on which of the following molecular targets?

options.D: Muscarinic M3 receptor on airway muscle

whyNot.A: Zileuton's target; blocking it would **lower urinary LTE4**, which stayed unchanged
whyNot.B: Inhibited indirectly by **corticosteroids** (she already takes one), and blocking it would also lower leukotriene output
whyNot.C: Target of **bronchodilators**; this tablet is **not a bronchodilator**
whyNot.D: Target of **inhaled** antimuscarinics (tiotropium, ipratropium), not a daily tablet

answer: Cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1 (CysLT1), blocked by montelukast
why: A drug that **leaves leukotriene E4 unchanged yet reduces symptoms** blocks the receptor, not the synthesis. **Montelukast** is a **CysLT1 receptor antagonist**, so leukotriene C4, D4 and E4 can no longer constrict the airway.

drug.name: Montelukast
drug.how: Blocks the CysLT1 receptor, so LTC4, LTD4 and LTE4 cannot cause bronchoconstriction, mucus and edema
drug.use: Asthma controller, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, allergic rhinitis
drug.watch: Neuropsychiatric events (boxed warning); may unmask eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis when steroids are reduced

idea.rule: Leukotriene drugs differ by where they block: receptor (montelukast, zafirlukast) or synthesis (zileuton).
also: Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase, lowering LTB4 and cysteinyl leukotrienes; check liver enzymes
Glucocorticoids reduce phospholipase A2 activity and so all arachidonate products
LTC4, LTD4 and LTE4 constrict bronchi and raise mucus; LTB4 attracts neutrophils
